items.title: Junior Mance Part II interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 18, 1999 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Gene Ammons, we played in a local big band called Jimmy Dale’s big band in Chicago.

ctx.x: Yeah, in fact I hear stories about guys who used to accidentally lose parts from things that got too difficult.

Oh yeah. You remember the famous baritone player Serge Chaloff, he played with Woody Herman. Well Serge was a wonderful baritone player but he memorized the whole book. But he had a habit of coming to work late or coming back after the intermission too late, and Woody was getting sick of it, and told him next time you’re going to get fired, next time you’re late. And Serge showed up late and Woody fired him right there, or gave him his two weeks’ notice. So the bus was traveling you know. And so they were…
That was nasty. I think I heard a follow up or something about Woody Herman getting back to him, something in the Bill Crow book. Pretty nasty actually.

items.title: Junior Mance Part I interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, New York City, New York, July 27, 1995…
items.q: I got my bebop chops from Albert Ammons’ son, Gene Ammons. I joined his band when I was seventeen.

ctx.x: Well I was listening to an interview of yours on one of your records in “Jazzspeak,” and you were talking about how you learned from your father and —

In a sense, yeah. My father never played piano professionally. When I was oh I guess around five years old we moved to this apartment in Evanston, which is actually where I grew up, in the suburbs of Chicago. And whoever was there before us, just left this big old upright, you know, I mean big too. Uprights were like about six feet tall it seems like. It was probably too big and the person didn’t want to be bothered with moving it elsewhere. So my father had a good ear for music. He liked music. He listened, and…

years ago, he was more or less a cocktail lounge type piano player. But the knowledge he had, his heroes, were like Art Tatum, Teddy Wilson, Earl Hines in that order. You know so that was, those were the guys that I heard early in my career. And so what better three to listen to, to start off, you know, and he would play their records, you know like 78s back in those days you know, and they also put out these books of their solos, which some of them were impossible to read. I’m still not the greatest sight reader…
